INTRODUCTION
Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is defined as an acute infection of the pulmonary
parenchyma in a patient who has acquired the infection in the community, as distinguished
from hospital-acquired (nosocomial) pneumonia. CAP is a common and potentially serious
illness with considerable morbidity.
The inpatient treatment of CAP and hospital-acquired pneumonia in children >28 days old will
be reviewed here.
Our recommendations are generally consistent with practice guidelines provided by  the
Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society/Infectious Diseases Society of America and the British
Thoracic Society [1,2]. (See 'Society guideline links' below.)
Other topics related to CAP in children and management of pneumonia in neonates are
discussed separately:

This topic discusses treatment for three categories of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP).
These categories are defined as follows:

●  Nonsevere uncomplicated pneumonia – In this context, nonsevere pneumonia refers to
   pneumonia that requires hospitalization for one or more indications (eg, age, level of
   respiratory distress, inability of the caregiver to care for the child at home) (                                     table 1). This
   category of treatment is only intended for children without pneumonia complications. (See
   'Nonsevere uncomplicated pneumonia' below.)

●  Severe uncomplicated pneumonia – Children with severe pneumonia are in moderate to
   severe distress (eg, nasal flaring, grunting, altered mental status, peripheral oxygen
   saturation [SpO2] <90 percent in room air, capillary refill ≥2 seconds) (                  table 2). This
   category of treatment is only intended for children without pneumonia complications. (See
   'Severe uncomplicated pneumonia' below.)

●  Complicated pneumonia – Complicated pneumonia refers to pneumonia associated with
   parapneumonic effusion/empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, or lung abscess. Complicated
   pneumonia can be associated with either nonsevere or severe clinical manifestations.
   Complicated pneumonia requires broader antimicrobial therapy than is used for
   uncomplicated pneumonia. It also may require invasive interventions to drain effusions or
   remove necrotic tissue. (See 'Complicated pneumonia' below and "Management and
   prognosis of parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children".)

Pneumonia in children >28 days old: Inpatient treatment - UpToDate

This topic discusses treatment for three categories of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). These categories are defined as follows:

- **Nonsevere uncomplicated pneumonia** – In this context, nonsevere pneumonia refers to pneumonia that requires hospitalization for one or more indications (eg, age, level of respiratory distress, inability of the caregiver to care for the child at home) (<u>table 1</u>). This category of treatment is only intended for children without pneumonia complications. (See '<u>Nonsevere uncomplicated pneumonia</u>' below.)

- **Severe uncomplicated pneumonia** – Children with severe pneumonia are in moderate to severe distress (eg, nasal flaring, grunting, altered mental status, peripheral oxygen saturation [SpO<sub>2</sub>] <90 percent in room air, capillary refill ≥2 seconds) (<u>table 2</u>). This category of treatment is only intended for children without pneumonia complications. (See '<u>Severe uncomplicated pneumonia</u>' below.)

- **Complicated pneumonia** – Complicated pneumonia refers to pneumonia associated with parapneumonic effusion/empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, or lung abscess. Complicated pneumonia can be associated with either nonsevere or severe clinical manifestations. Complicated pneumonia requires broader antimicrobial therapy than is used for uncomplicated pneumonia. It also may require invasive interventions to drain effusions or remove necrotic tissue. (See '<u>Complicated pneumonia</u>' below and "<u>Management and prognosis of parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children</u>").

# INDICATIONS FOR HOSPITALIZATION

- **General indications for hospital admission** – The decision to hospitalize a child with pneumonia is individualized based on age, underlying medical problems, and severity of illness. Indications for hospitalization include (<u>table 1</u>) [1-3]:

  - Young age – Hospitalization is often warranted for infants <3 to 6 months of age, unless a viral etiology or *Chlamydia trachomatis* is suspected and the infant is minimally symptomatic and not hypoxemic.
  
  - Hypoxemia (peripheral oxygen saturation [SpO<sub>2</sub>] <90 percent in room air).
  
  - Dehydration or inability to maintain hydration orally; inability to feed in an infant.

| Indication                                                            | Comment                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Most children <1 to 6 months of age                                   | Exception: a viral etiology or Chlamydia trachomatis is suspected and the child is relatively asymptomatic without hypoxemia                                                                      |
| Inability to care for at home                                         | Any child whose caregiver(s) cannot provide appropriate care or follow the management instructions                                                                                                |
| Hypoxia                                                               | SpO₂ < 90% on room air                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Dehydration                                                           | Inability to maintain oral hydration or inability to feed an infant                                                                                                                               |
| Moderate to severe respiratory distress                               | Examples: RR > 70 (breaths per minute for infants <12 months of age, RR > 50 breaths per minute for children >12 months of age, retractions, nasal flaring, difficulty breathing, agonal grunting |
| Toxic appearance                                                      | Toxic appearance is more common in bacterial pneumonia and may suggest more severe disease                                                                                                        |
| Underlying conditions that predispose to a more severe course         | Examples: cardiopulmonary disease, genetic syndromes, neurocognitive disorders                                                                                                                    |
| Underlying conditions that may be exacerbated by pneumonia            | Examples: metabolic disorder                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Underlying conditions that may adversely affect response to treatment | Examples: immunocompromised host                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Complications of pneumonia present                                    | Examples: effusion/empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, lung abscess                                                                                                                                   |
| Resistance or confirmation of a pathogen that has increased virulence | Examples: streptococcus pneumoniae, group A Streptococcus                                                                                                                                         |
| Failure of outpatient therapy                                         | Continued lack of response within 48 to 72 hours of antibiotic change                                                                                                                             |

3/18/26, 5:06 PM                 Pneumonia in children >28 days old: Inpatient treatment - UpToDate
   •  Moderate to severe respiratory distress – This includes tachypnea (respiratory rate >70
      breaths per minute [bpm] for infants <12 months of age and >50 bpm for older children),
      retractions, nasal flaring, difficulty breathing, apnea, and/or grunting.

   •  Toxic appearance – Toxic appearance is more common in bacterial pneumonia and may
      suggest a more severe course [4].

   •  Underlying conditions that may predispose to a more serious course of pneumonia (eg,
      heart disease, lung disease, immune deficiency, genetic syndromes, neuromuscular
      disorders) or may be worsened by pneumonia (eg, metabolic disorder).

   •  Complications (eg, parapneumonic effusion/empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, lung
      abscess). (See 'Complicated pneumonia' below and "Management and prognosis of
      parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children".)

   •  Suspected or confirmed pathogen associated with high likelihood of causing severe
      and/or rapidly progressive infection (eg, Staphylococcus aureus or group A Streptococcus
      [GAS]).

   •  Failure of outpatient therapy (worsening or lack of response within 48 to 72 hours of
      antibiotic change).
   Most children who require hospitalization for pneumonia can be managed in the general
   inpatient pediatric unit. Indications for intensive care unit admission are outlined below.

●  Pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission – Admission to the PICU is generally
   warranted for children with any of the following [1,2]:

   •  Severe respiratory distress (eg, marked retractions, dyspnea, nasal flaring, grunting)

   •  Need for advanced respiratory support (mechanical ventilation, noninvasive ventilation
      [NIV])

   •  Moderate to severe hypoxemia (eg, requiring a high fraction of inspired oxygen [FiO2] to
      maintain SpO2 >92 percent [eg, FiO2 >0.5])

   •  Recurrent episodes of apnea

   •  Depressed or altered mental status

   •  Hemodynamic instability or shock (eg, progressive tachycardia, lactic acidosis, and/or
      hypotension despite fluid resuscitation)

   •  Underlying medical condition that places the child at high risk for severe/complicated
      illness (eg, sickle cell disease, primary immune deficiency)

- Moderate to severe respiratory distress – This includes tachypnea (respiratory rate >70 breaths per minute [bpm] for infants <12 months of age and >50 bpm for older children), retractions, nasal flaring, difficulty breathing, apnea, and/or grunting.

- Toxic appearance – Toxic appearance is more common in bacterial pneumonia and may suggest a more severe course [[4]].

- Underlying conditions that may predispose to a more serious course of pneumonia (eg, heart disease, lung disease, immune deficiency, genetic syndromes, neuromuscular disorders) or may be worsened by pneumonia (eg, metabolic disorder).

- Complications (eg, parapneumonic effusion/empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, lung abscess). (See 'Complicated pneumonia' below and "Management and prognosis of parapneumonic effusion and empyema in children").)

- Suspected or confirmed pathogen associated with high likelihood of causing severe and/or rapidly progressive infection (eg, *Staphylococcus aureus* or group A *Streptococcus* [GAS]).

- Failure of outpatient therapy (worsening or lack of response within 48 to 72 hours of antibiotic change).

Most children who require hospitalization for pneumonia can be managed in the general inpatient pediatric unit. Indications for intensive care unit admission are outlined below.

- **Pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission** – Admission to the PICU is generally warranted for children with any of the following [[1,2]]:

- Severe respiratory distress (eg, marked retractions, dyspnea, nasal flaring, grunting)

- Need for advanced respiratory support (mechanical ventilation, noninvasive ventilation [NIV])

- Moderate to severe hypoxemia (eg, requiring a high fraction of inspired oxygen [FiO<sub>2</sub>] to maintain SpO<sub>2</sub> >92 percent [eg, FiO<sub>2</sub> >0.5]))

- Recurrent episodes of apnea

- Depressed or altered mental status

- Hemodynamic instability or shock (eg, progressive tachycardia, lactic acidosis, and/or hypotension despite fluid resuscitation)

- Underlying medical condition that places the child at high risk for severe/complicated illness (eg, sickle cell disease, primary immune deficiency)

INFECTION CONTROL MEASURES

Rapid diagnostic tests — If possible, rapid diagnostic tests should be performed at the time
of admission to facilitate patient cohorting and other infection control decisions. We prefer
rapid diagnostic tests to cultures because of their general availability, and their results are
reported sooner. (See "Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and
diagnosis", section on 'Rapid diagnostic testing'.)
General measures

●  Standard precautions – Standard precautions include hand hygiene and, if exposure to
   infectious material is anticipated (eg, purulent wound, respiratory secretions), the use of
   personal protective equipment. Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to
   prevent the spread of infection. Guidelines for hand hygiene in health care settings can be
   accessed through the  Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

●  Additional infection control measures – Additional infection control measures for
   suspected respiratory pathogens depend on the likely pathogen. However, we favor
   simplifying the approach by placing all patients with suspected respiratory tract infection on
   both contact and droplet precautions. If measles or varicella are suspected, airborne
   precautions are also indicated.
   Once the results of rapid diagnostic tests or cultures are available, measures can be
   narrowed as follows [5,6]:

   •  Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), parainfluenza, and human metapneumovirus – Contact
      precautions (ie, gown and gloves) and mask according to standard precautions

   •  Influenza, rhinovirus, group A Streptococcus (GAS; first 24 hours of treatment), and
      Mycoplasma pneumoniae – Droplet precautions (ie, mask within 3 feet)

   •  Adenovirus – Contact and droplet precautions

   •  Measles – Airborne precautions (ie, use of fit-tested N95 mask)

   •  Varicella – Airborne and contact precautions

   •  Methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) – Standard precautions

   •  Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) or other multidrug-resistant organisms – Contact
      and droplet precautions if exposed to respiratory secretions and use of dedicated patient
      equipment

**Rapid diagnostic tests** — If possible, rapid diagnostic tests should be performed at the time of admission to facilitate patient cohorting and other infection control decisions. (See "Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis", section on 'Rapid diagnostic testing'.)

## General measures

- **Standard precautions** – Standard precautions include hand hygiene and, if exposure to infectious material is anticipated (eg, purulent wound, respiratory secretions), the use of personal protective equipment. Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to prevent the spread of infection. Guidelines for hand hygiene in health care settings can be accessed through the 🔗 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

- **Additional infection control measures** – Additional infection control measures for suspected respiratory pathogens depend on the likely pathogen. However, we favor simplifying the approach by placing all patients with suspected respiratory tract infection on both contact and droplet precautions. If measles or varicella are suspected, airborne precautions are also indicated.

Once the results of rapid diagnostic tests or cultures are available, measures can be narrowed as follows [5,6]:

- Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), parainfluenza, and human metapneumovirus – Contact precautions (ie, gown and gloves) and mask according to standard precautions
- Influenza, rhinovirus, group A *Streptococcus* (GAS; first 24 hours of treatment), and *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* – Droplet precautions (ie, mask within 3 feet)
- Adenovirus – Contact and droplet precautions
- Measles – Airborne precautions (ie, use of fit-tested N95 mask)
- Varicella – Airborne and contact precautions
- Methicillin-susceptible *S. aureus* (MSSA) – Standard precautions
- Methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* (MRSA) or other multidrug-resistant organisms – Contact and droplet precautions if exposed to respiratory secretions and use of dedicated patient equipment

PRETREATMENT EVALUATION

●  Laboratory evaluation – The typical laboratory evaluation for children hospitalized with
   pneumonia includes a complete blood count (CBC) with differential, inflammatory markers,
   and serum electrolytes.

   •  CBC – When assessed in conjunction with other clinical, laboratory, and radiographic
      features, the white blood cell (WBC) count can sometimes be helpful in distinguishing
      between typical bacterial, atypical bacterial, and nonbacterial causes of pneumonia:
       -  An elevated WBC count (>15,000/microL) is suggestive of a typical bacterial etiology [7].
          However, children with M. pneumoniae, influenza, or adenovirus pneumonia may also
          have an elevated WBC count [8-10].
       -  A normal or reduced WBC count suggests a nonbacterial etiology. However, a severely
          ill patient with bacterial pneumonia may present with leukopenia with a predominance
          of immature cells.
       -  Peripheral eosinophilia is characteristic of afebrile pneumonia of infancy (typically
          caused by C. trachomatis). (See "Chlamydia trachomatis infections in newborns and
          young infants", section on 'Pneumonia'.)

   •  Inflammatory markers – Baseline inflammatory markers (eg, erythrocyte sedimentation
      rate [ESR], C-reactive protein [CRP], serum procalcitonin [PCT]) obtained at admission and
      followed by serial measurements during treatment may provide useful information about
      a patient's response to therapy [1,11-16]. They may also assist with clinical management
      decisions (eg, when to discontinue antimicrobial therapy). (See 'Duration of treatment'
      below.)
      Inflammatory marker levels do not reliably differentiate between typical bacterial,
      atypical bacterial, and viral pneumonia, but they may be helpful for assessing the
      likelihood of each. In a meta-analysis of observational studies in children, an elevated CRP
      and PCT performed better than an elevated WBC count in distinguishing bacterial from
      viral pneumonia; however, the sensitivity and specificity of approximately 70 and 65

   •  Serum electrolytes – We suggest measuring serum electrolytes in all children requiring

●  Radiographic evaluation – Children who are admitted to the hospital with pneumonia
   should have chest radiographs to confirm the diagnosis and assess for complications (eg,

●  Microbiologic testing – Children who are admitted to the hospital for CAP should undergo
   microbiologic testing that includes rapid diagnostic testing (see 'Rapid diagnostic tests'

   culture. The microbiologic evaluation is discussed in detail separately. (See "Community-
   acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis", section on 'Microbiologic
   testing'.)
   Microbiologic testing is necessary in all hospitalized children with CAP since the clinical,
   laboratory. and radiologic features do not reliably distinguish between different etiologies.
   (See "Pneumonia in children: Epidemiology, pathogenesis, and etiology", section on
   'Etiologic agents'.)

SUPPORTIVE AND ADJUNCTIVE CARE

Antipyresis and analgesia — Fever and pleuritic chest pain should be treated with
antipyretics and/or analgesics (eg, acetaminophen, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug
[NSAID]). Fever can increase tachypnea and work of breathing in infants and children with
pneumonia. Pleuritic chest pain can lead to shallow breathing and impaired ability to cough.
Opioid analgesia does not play any role in this setting unless the child has a chest tube in
place and experiences breakthrough pain while receiving parenteral ketorolac.
Respiratory support — Children hospitalized with pneumonia should receive respiratory
support as indicated by their clinical condition [1,2].
For children with hypoxemia, we suggest titrating supplemental oxygen therapy to maintain
peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) ≥92 percent. Other experts use different targets for
supplemental oxygen. Gentle bulb suctioning of the nares may help reduce oxygen
requirements in infants and children whose nares are blocked with secretions. Minimal

Microbiologic testing is necessary in all hospitalized children with CAP since the clinical, laboratory. and radiologic features do not reliably distinguish between different etiologies.
(See <u>"Pneumonia in children: Epidemiology, pathogenesis, and etiology"</u>, section on '<u>Etiologic agents</u>'.))

## **SUPPORTIVE AND ADJUNCTIVE CARE**

**Antipyresis and analgesia** — Fever and pleuritic chest pain should be treated with antipyretics and/or analgesics (eg, <u>acetaminophen</u>, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug [NSAID]). Fever can increase tachypnea and work of breathing in infants and children with pneumonia. Pleuritic chest pain can lead to shallow breathing and impaired ability to cough. Opioid analgesia does not play any role in this setting unless the child has a chest tube in place and experiences breakthrough pain while receiving parenteral <u>ketorolac</u>.

**Respiratory support** — Children hospitalized with pneumonia should receive respiratory support as indicated by their clinical condition [<u>1,2</u>].

For children with hypoxemia, we suggest titrating supplemental oxygen therapy to maintain peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO<sub>2</sub>) ≥92 percent. Other experts use different targets for supplemental oxygen. Gentle bulb suctioning of the nares may help reduce oxygen requirements in infants and children whose nares are blocked with secretions. effectiveness of various CPT interventions including conventional CPT with and without positive expiratory pressure, CPAP (nasal and bubble), and assisted autogenic drainage in children hospitalized with pneumonia [24]. Of the five trials reporting changes in SpO<sub>2</sub> after the CPT intervention, two trials reported improvements in SpO<sub>2</sub> whereas three trials did not detect any improvement. There was little to no difference in length of hospital stay between children who did or did not receive CPT (based on four trials).

- **Adjunctive glucocorticoid therapy** – We do not routinely provide glucocorticoid therapy to children hospitalized with pneumonia. Although some data suggest benefit, trials are limited, and more data are needed before this practice can be adopted as routine.

A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis identified three small pediatric trials assessing the effect of systemic glucocorticoid therapy in children with *M. pneumoniae* pneumonia (two trials) or CAP (one trial) [25]. There were no deaths among the 225 children enrolled in these trials. The time to clinical cure was faster for children assigned to glucocorticoid therapy compared with those in the control group (mean difference 1.6 days, 95% CI 0.6-2.6 days). Children receiving glucocorticoid therapy were also less likely to have early clinical failure (defined as radiographic progression or clinical instability at day 5 through 8) compared with those in the control group (relative risk [RR] 0.41, 95% CI 0.24-0.70). However, the clinical failure rate in the control group was unusually high (66 percent) and not consistent with contemporary practice in resource-abundant settings. Thus, this finding may not be generalizable to other settings.

In a retrospective study of 2244 children treated for CAP in the outpatient setting, 13 percent received adjunctive glucocorticoid therapy, most of whom had underlying asthma [26]. Among children without underlying asthma, use of adjunctive glucocorticoids was associated with increased likelihood of having an unplanned acute care visit for respiratory complaints within 14 days of the CAP diagnosis. This finding suggests that glucocorticoid therapy may have a detrimental effect in children with nonsevere CAP in the absence of underlying asthma.

Additional large, well-designed pediatric trials are needed to clarify the role of adjunctive glucocorticoids in treating CAP.

The features often overlap, and they do not           Table 4 - larger image below

guiding empiric therapy pending results of microbiologic testing.
We suggest that clinicians use their best judgment as to whether the child's overall clinical
picture (including the presentation, laboratory results, and radiographic findings) is most
consistent with typical bacterial pneumonia, atypical bacterial pneumonia, a mixed picture,
or a viral illness (  table 4).

●  If the clinical picture is most consistent with typical bacterial pneumonia (eg, lobar
   consolidation on chest radiograph with high fever and elevated inflammatory markers),
   empiric therapy should target common bacterial causes of CAP (eg, Streptococcus
   pneumoniae, group A Streptococcus [GAS], Haemophilus influenzae), as discussed below.
   (See 'Age-based regimens for nonsevere uncomplicated CAP' below.)

●  If the clinical picture is most consistent with atypical bacterial pneumonia (eg, myalgias,
   conjunctivitis, sore throat, rash), empiric therapy consists of a macrolide (eg,
   azithromycin) to cover atypical bacterial pathogens (M. pneumoniae, Chlamydia
   pneumoniae).

●  If the clinical picture is mixed, combination therapy is generally appropriate (ie, an agent
   that covers typical bacterial pathogens plus a macrolide to cover atypical pathogens).

●  If the clinical picture is most consistent with a viral infection and there is no concern for
   bacterial coinfection, antibiotic therapy is not necessary. Antiviral therapy should be
   provided if a treatable viral etiology is identified (eg, influenza or coronavirus disease
   2019 [COVID-19]). For other viral pathogens (eg, respiratory syncytial virus [RSV],
   rhinovirus, adenovirus), treatment is supportive. (See 'Viral pathogens' below and
   'Confirmed viral etiology' below.)
While we suggest using this approach to help guide the initial choice of empiric therapy,
clinicians should recognize that making these judgments is not an exact science. Therefore,
it is important to regularly reevaluate the patient to assess their response to therapy and
modify treatment if necessary. (See 'Response to therapy' below.)

The features often overlap, and they do not reliably distinguish between the different etiologies. Nevertheless, they can be helpful in guiding empiric therapy pending results of microbiologic testing.

We suggest that clinicians use their best judgment as to whether the child's overall clinical picture (including the presentation, laboratory results, and radiographic findings) is most consistent with typical bacterial pneumonia, atypical bacterial pneumonia, a mixed picture, or a viral illness (<u>table 4</u>).

- If the clinical picture is most consistent with typical bacterial pneumonia (eg, lobar consolidation on chest radiograph with high fever and elevated inflammatory markers), empiric therapy should target common bacterial causes of CAP (eg, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, group A *Streptococcus* [GAS], *Haemophilus influenzae*), as discussed below. (See <u>'Age-based regimens for nonsevere uncomplicated CAP'</u> below.)

- If the clinical picture is most consistent with atypical bacterial pneumonia (eg, myalgias, conjunctivitis, sore throat, rash), empiric therapy consists of a macrolide (eg, <u>azithromycin</u>) to cover atypical bacterial pathogens (*M. pneumoniae*, *Chlamydia pneumoniae*).

- If the clinical picture is mixed, combination therapy is generally appropriate (ie, an agent that covers typical bacterial pathogens plus a macrolide to cover atypical pathogens).

- If the clinical picture is most consistent with a viral infection and there is no concern for bacterial coinfection, antibiotic therapy is not necessary. Antiviral therapy should be provided if a treatable viral etiology is identified (eg, influenza or coronavirus disease 2019 [COVID-19]). For other viral pathogens (eg, respiratory syncytial virus [RSV], rhinovirus, adenovirus), treatment is supportive. (See <u>'Viral pathogens'</u> below and <u>'Confirmed viral etiology'</u> below.)

While we suggest using this approach to help guide the initial choice of empiric therapy, clinicians should recognize that making these judgments is not an exact science. Therefore, it is important to regularly reevaluate the patient to assess their response to therapy and modify treatment if necessary. (See <u>'Response to therapy'</u> below.)

3/18/26, 5:06 PM    Pneumonia in children >28 days old: Inpatient treatment - UpToDate
    table 3B). Infants at this age are not fully immunized against S. pneumoniae and H.
influenzae type b (Hib). Third-generation cephalosporins provide empiric coverage for
penicillin-resistant strains of S. pneumoniae (PRSP) and beta-lactamase-producing strains
of invasive H. influenzae [4,28-30].
Afebrile well-appearing infants between the ages of two weeks and four months may
have pneumonia caused by C. trachomatis (sometimes called afebrile pneumonia of
infancy), which is characterized by insidious onset of nasal congestion and possibly
conjunctivitis, followed by gradual development of staccato cough and tachypnea. C.
trachomatis pneumonia is typically a mild illness, and most affected infants do not require
hospitalization unless their illness is associated with dehydration or other complications.
C. trachomatis pneumonia is treated with macrolide antibiotics (eg, azithromycin), as
discussed separately. (See "Chlamydia trachomatis infections in newborns and young
infants", section on 'Pneumonia'.)
Infants and children 6 months to <4 years — S. pneumoniae is the most common
bacterial cause of pneumonia in this age group. Other bacterial etiologies include
Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS), Hib (if not fully immunized), other typeable non-b and
nontypeable H. influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis [2,4,28,31-35].
For infants ≥6 months and children <4 years, the choice of empiric antibiotic(s) depends
on immunization status and community prevalence of PRSP. Local rates of PRSP are
usually available from the antibiogram of the microbiology laboratory at the treating
hospital.
Our suggested approach is as follows:

 ●  For children with presumed typical bacterial CAP who are fully immunized (        table 5)
    and live in a community with rates of PRSP <25 percent, we suggest ampicillin or
    penicillin G [1,36,37]. The table provides dosing guidance (  table 3B).
    For certain patients, oral amoxicillin may be a reasonable alternative, as discussed
    below. (See 'Parenteral therapy preferred for most patients' below.)

 ●  For children who are not fully immunized or live in a community with rates of PRSP ≥25
    percent, we suggest treatment with ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime, where available) rather
    than ampicillin or penicillin G.

 ●  For children with findings consistent with atypical pneumonia (eg, myalgias,
    conjunctivitis, sore throat, rash, sick contact within past month), we suggest adding a
    macrolide antibiotic (eg, azithromycin) to the empiric regimen. The incidence of M.
    pneumoniae in children hospitalized for pneumonia is rising [38].

📋 **table 3B**). Infants at this age are not fully immunized against *S. pneumoniae* and *H. influenzae* type b (Hib). Third-generation cephalosporins provide empiric coverage for penicillin-resistant strains of *S. pneumoniae* (PRSP) and beta-lactamase-producing strains of invasive *H. influenzae* [4,<u>28-30</u>].

Afebrile well-appearing infants between the ages of two weeks and four months may have pneumonia caused by *C. trachomatis* (sometimes called afebrile pneumonia of infancy), which is characterized by insidious onset of nasal congestion and possibly conjunctivitis, followed by gradual development of staccato cough and tachypnea. *C. trachomatis* pneumonia is typically a mild illness, and most affected infants do not require hospitalization unless their illness is associated with dehydration or other complications. *C. trachomatis* pneumonia is treated with macrolide antibiotics (eg, <u>azithromycin</u>), as discussed separately. (See "<u>Chlamydia trachomatis infections in newborns and young infants</u>", section on 'Pneumonia'.)

**Infants and children 6 months to <4 years** — *S. pneumoniae* is the most common bacterial cause of pneumonia in this age group. Other bacterial etiologies include *Streptococcus pyogenes* (GAS), Hib (if not fully immunized), other typeable non-b and nontypeable *H. influenzae*, and *Moraxella catarrhalis* [<u>2,4,28,31-35</u>].

For infants ≥6 months and children <4 years, the choice of empiric antibiotic(s) depends on immunization status and community prevalence of PRSP. Local rates of PRSP are usually available from the antibiogram of the microbiology laboratory at the treating hospital.

Our suggested approach is as follows:

- For children with presumed typical bacterial CAP who are fully immunized (<u>📋 table 5</u>) and live in a community with rates of PRSP <25 percent, we suggest <u>ampicillin</u> or <u>penicillin G</u> [1,<u>36,37</u>]. The table provides dosing guidance (<u>📋 table 3B</u>).

For certain patients, oral <u>amoxicillin</u> may be a reasonable alternative, as discussed below. (See '<u>Parenteral therapy preferred for most patients</u>' below.)

- For children who are not fully immunized or live in a community with rates of PRSP ≥25 percent, we suggest treatment with <u>ceftriaxone</u> (or <u>cefotaxime</u>, where available) rather than <u>ampicillin</u> or <u>penicillin G</u>.

- For children with findings consistent with atypical pneumonia (eg, myalgias, conjunctivitis, sore throat, rash, sick contact within past month), we suggest adding a macrolide antibiotic (eg, <u>azithromycin</u>) to the empiric regimen. The incidence of *M. pneumoniae* in children hospitalized for pneumonia is rising [<u>38</u>].

    alternative (   table 3B). For those with contraindications to beta-lactam antibiotics,
    clindamycin or levofloxacin are acceptable alternatives.
Based on the available data, there does not appear to be any advantage to using
combined beta-lactam plus macrolide therapy in children without clinical features of
atypical pneumonia [39]. A prospective population-based study of 1418 children
hospitalized with radiographically confirmed CAP did not detect any differences in length
of stay, intensive care admission, rehospitalization, or self-reported recovery in children
who received combination therapy compared with those who received beta-lactam
monotherapy [39].
Children ≥4 years — Atypical bacterial pathogens (eg, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae)
cause pneumonia more commonly in children ≥4 years old than in younger children. In
addition, the typical bacterial CAP pathogens (S. pneumoniae, GAS, H. influenzae) are also
common in this age group.
For children ≥4 years of age, the choice of empiric antibiotic(s) depends on immunization
status, community rates of PRSP, and suspicion for atypical bacterial infection.

   In addition to its excellent gram-negative spectrum, levofloxacin is active against a
   number of other pathogens responsible for CAP, including beta-lactam-susceptible and
   nonsusceptible S. pneumoniae, M. pneumoniae (including macrolide-resistant M.

●  For children ≥4 years old and adolescents who have a contraindication to beta-lactam
   antibiotics (eg, history of IgE-mediated reaction or serious delayed reaction
   (                table 6)), levofloxacin is an acceptable alternative.
Parenteral therapy preferred for most patients — We suggest that children who require
hospitalization for treatment of pneumonia be treated initially with parenteral antibiotics
[1]. These children are typically not eating well and are receiving intravenous (IV) fluid
hydration. In this setting, provide IV antibiotic therapy rather than trying to administer oral
antibiotics to a sick child.
However, oral amoxicillin may be an acceptable alternative for infants and children who are
fully immunized against Hib and S. pneumoniae and have nonsevere, uncomplicated
pneumonia that is not thought to be due to S. aureus [43,44]. In a multicenter clinical trial in
which patients with uncomplicated nonsevere CAP were randomly assigned to treatment
with oral amoxicillin or IV penicillin G, clinical outcomes were similar in both groups [45].
The British Thoracic Society guidelines also suggest that oral antibiotics are safe and
effective for children hospitalized with pneumonia as long as they are able to tolerate oral
fluids, are not vomiting, and do not have signs of septicemia or complicated pneumonia [2].
Suspicion for specific organisms
S. aureus — Children with pneumonia caused by S. aureus are typically toxic appearing with
high fever and a severe, rapidly progressing illness. Staphylococcal pneumonia may be
preceded by a viral respiratory tract infection (especially influenza) and may be associated
with complications (eg, parapneumonic effusion/empyema, necrotizing pneumonia, lung
abscess) [46,47]. For this reason, antistaphylococcal coverage is included in the empiric
regimen for children with complicated pneumonia or severe pneumonia requiring intensive
care management, as discussed below. (See 'Severe uncomplicated pneumonia' below and
'Complicated pneumonia' below.)
Additional guidance for selecting empiric antistaphylococcal coverage in children with
suspected invasive S. aureus infections is summarized in the table (     table 7) and discussed
in detail separately. (See "Staphylococcus aureus in children: Overview of treatment of
invasive infections", section on 'Choice of therapy'.)

   Testing for nasal carriage of methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA)/methicillin-resistant S.
   aureus (MRSA) by culture or molecular tests may be helpful in reducing the use of anti-
   MSSA/MRSA therapy in the treatment of nonsevere uncomplicated pneumonia [48-50]. A
   negative result has a negative predictive value of approximately 95 percent for excluding
   MRSA pneumonia. Nevertheless, clinical judgment should be used to determine whether
   further testing is needed to completely rule out MRSA pneumonia.
   Viral pathogens — Most children <5 years of age who are admitted to the hospital with
   pneumonia have viral pneumonia (eg, RSV, rhinovirus, adenovirus) [51]. This is particularly
   true in the absence of a lobar (or lobular) infiltrate and pleural effusion [4]. Viral pneumonia
   does not require empiric antibiotic therapy unless a mixed bacterial infection or secondary
   bacterial infection is suspected. Importantly, up to one-half of CAP in children may be of a
   mixed viral/bacterial etiology.
   Common treatable viral causes of pneumonia include influenza and COVID-19. These are
   readily detectable with rapid diagnostic tests. (See 'Rapid diagnostic tests' above and
   'Confirmed viral etiology' below.)
   If a child is hospitalized during influenza season and results of rapid diagnostic testing for
   influenza are not readily available, empiric antiviral therapy (eg, oseltamivir) should be
   started pending laboratory confirmation. (See "Seasonal influenza in children:
   Management", section on 'Indications and preferred regimens'.)
   If influenza is complicated by secondary bacterial pneumonia, empiric antibiotic therapy
   should include coverage for S. aureus, including MRSA. Coinfection with influenza and S.
   aureus is particularly severe and can be rapidly fatal. (See "Seasonal influenza in children:
   Clinical features and diagnosis", section on 'S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, or S. aureus
   coinfection'.)
   Other considerations for antiviral therapy are discussed below. (See 'Confirmed viral
   etiology' below.)
Aspiration pneumonia — For empiric treatment of aspiration pneumonia, we suggest
ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin [52]. The former provides coverage for oral anaerobes as
well as the usual bacterial causes of CAP (eg, S. pneumoniae, GAS, MSSA, H. influenzae). The
latter's coverage is similar, except it lacks coverage against H influenzae, and its GAS, S.
pneumoniae, and MSSA coverage is not as broad.
Clindamycin is preferred if MRSA is suspected and the prevalence of clindamycin resistance in
the community is <15 percent [53] or if the patient has a contraindication to beta-lactam
antibiotics (eg, history of IgE-mediated reaction or severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction
(  table 6)).

Testing for nasal carriage of methicillin-susceptible *S. aureus* (MSSA)/methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* (MRSA) by culture or molecular tests may be helpful in reducing the use of anti-MSSA/MRSA therapy in the treatment of nonsevere uncomplicated pneumonia [<48-50>]. A negative result has a negative predictive value of approximately 95 percent for excluding MRSA pneumonia. Nevertheless, clinical judgment should be used to determine whether further testing is needed to completely rule out MRSA pneumonia.

**Viral pathogens** — Most children <5 years of age who are admitted to the hospital with pneumonia have viral pneumonia (eg, RSV, rhinovirus, adenovirus) [51]. This is particularly true in the absence of a lobar (or lobular) infiltrate and pleural effusion [4]. Viral pneumonia does not require empiric antibiotic therapy unless a mixed bacterial infection or secondary bacterial infection is suspected. Importantly, up to one-half of CAP in children may be of a mixed viral/bacterial etiology.

Common treatable viral causes of pneumonia include influenza and COVID-19. These are readily detectable with rapid diagnostic tests. (See '<u>Rapid diagnostic tests</u>' above and <u>'Confirmed viral etiology'</u> below.)

If a child is hospitalized during influenza season and results of rapid diagnostic testing for influenza are not readily available, empiric antiviral therapy (eg, oseltamivir) should be started pending laboratory confirmation. (See "<u>Seasonal influenza in children: Management</u>", section on '<u>Indications and preferred regimens</u>'.))

If influenza is complicated by secondary bacterial pneumonia, empiric antibiotic therapy should include coverage for *S. aureus*, including MRSA. Coinfection with influenza and *S. aureus* is particularly severe and can be rapidly fatal. (See "<u>Seasonal influenza in children: Clinical features and diagnosis</u>", section on '<u>S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, or S. aureus coinfection</u>'.))

Other considerations for antiviral therapy are discussed below. (See '<u>Confirmed viral etiology</u>' below.)

**Aspiration pneumonia** — For empiric treatment of aspiration pneumonia, we suggest ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin [52]. The former provides coverage for oral anaerobes as well as the usual bacterial causes of CAP (eg, *S. pneumoniae*, GAS, MSSA, *H. influenzae*). The latter's coverage is similar, except it lacks coverage against *H influenzae*, and its GAS, *S. pneumoniae*, and MSSA coverage is not as broad.

Clindamycin is preferred if MRSA is suspected and the prevalence of clindamycin resistance in the community is <15 percent [53] or if the patient has a contraindication to beta-lactam antibiotics (eg, history of IgE-mediated reaction or severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction (📊 table 6)).

In neurologically compromised older adolescents prone to aspiration events, empiric treatment with a fluoroquinolone (eg, <u>moxifloxacin</u> 400 mg once daily) is a reasonable alternative. Moxifloxacin also has activity against anaerobic bacteria and both the usual typical and atypical bacterial causes of CAP.

## **Severe uncomplicated pneumonia** — For children with severe pneumonia (<u>table 2</u>), we base the choice of empiric regimen on whether the child is critically ill (ie, requiring admission to the pediatric intensive care unit [PICU]). Indications for PICU care are discussed above. (See '<u>Indications for hospitalization</u>' above.)

- **Severe CAP not requiring PICU admission** – For children with severe CAP (<u>table 2</u>) who do not require admission to the PICU, we suggest combination empiric therapy with a third-generation cephalosporin (eg, <u>ceftriaxone</u> or <u>cefotaxime</u>) **plus** a macrolide (eg, <u>azithromycin</u>) (<u>table 3A-B</u>). Combination therapy improves coverage for resistant organisms and mixed bacterial/atypical bacterial infections.

If there is concern for *S. aureus*, options include (see '<u>S. aureus</u>' above):

- Adding either <u>vancomycin</u> or <u>clindamycin</u> (depending upon local susceptibility patterns) to a combination of third-generation cephalosporin and macrolide **or**
- Combination therapy with <u>ceftaroline</u> plus <u>azithromycin</u>

If the child is hospitalized during influenza season, antiviral therapy for influenza (eg, <u>oseltamivir</u>) may also be warranted. If results of rapid diagnostic testing for influenza are not readily available, empiric therapy should be started pending laboratory confirmation. (See "<u>Seasonal influenza in children: Management</u>", section on '<u>Antiviral therapy</u>'.)

- **Severe CAP requiring PICU admission** – Critically ill children requiring PICU care for severe pneumonia require broad-spectrum empiric therapy that provides coverage for potential beta-lactam resistance and MRSA.

We suggest the following regimen (<u>table 3A-B</u>) [54-56]:

- <u>Vancomycin</u> (<u>table 8</u>) **plus**
- <u>Nafcillin</u> or <u>oxacillin</u> **plus**

   Vancomycin is reserved for patients who are allergic to clindamycin or who are living in
   communities with a clindamycin-resistant S. aureus prevalence ≥15 percent (hospital
   thresholds vary). Additional considerations include community MRSA prevalence >25
   percent and severe illness. Kidney function and/or use of other nephrotoxic agents and
   turnaround time for susceptibility results also factor into the decision. Additional details,
   including vancomycin monitoring, are discussed above. (See 'Severe uncomplicated
   pneumonia' above.)
   Monotherapy with ceftaroline (  table 3B) is an alternative if there are contraindications to
   penicillin G, ampicillin, clindamycin, or vancomycin. In a multicenter randomized trial of 40
   children with complicated community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (only one had
   documented MRSA), clinical cure rates at the end of treatment with ceftaroline
   monotherapy were similar to combination ceftriaxone and vancomycin (approximately 80
   percent) [57]. (See "Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and
   diagnosis", section on 'Complications'.)
   In addition to antibiotic therapy, children with moderate to large parapneumonic effusions
   or an empyema require invasive procedures to drain the pleural fluid. This is discussed
   separately. (See "Management and prognosis of parapneumonic effusion and empyema in
   children".)

   child requires coverage for the common typical bacterial etiologies of CAP (S. pneumoniae,

   event.
   We suggest one of the following regimens (  table 3B):

   above.)

antipseudomonal beta-lactam antibiotic (for gram-negative pathogens) with another agent
that covers gram-positive pathogens with or without anaerobic coverage.

●  Piperacillin-tazobactam 300 mg/kg per day IV in divided four doses (maximum 12 g/day),
   or

●  Meropenem 60 mg/kg per day IV in three divided doses (maximum 6 g/day), or

●  Cefepime 150 mg/kg per day in three divided doses (maximum 4 g/day), if no suspicion of
   an aspiration event
Vancomycin or linezolid is added to the above regimen if MRSA is suspected based on
known patient colonization or the epidemiology of the patient's unit (  table 3B and
   table 8). (See 'S. aureus' above.)
Piperacillin-tazobactam may not be preferred for gram-negative coverage if vancomycin is
added because the combination of vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam has been
associated with increased risk of acute kidney injury [58,59]. However, this risk must be
weighed against the development of meropenem resistance, particularly in closed units.
If the patient is known to be colonized with a gram-negative organism that produces an
extended-spectrum or AmpC beta-lactamase, we suggest therapy with meropenem alone.
If the patient is neutropenic or in septic shock, we suggest the addition of amikacin 15 to
22.5 mg/kg per day divided in one or three divided doses.
Decisions about appropriate empiric antimicrobial therapy should be made in consultation
with an infectious disease specialist.
Immunocompromised host — An aggressive approach to specific microbial diagnosis is
indicated in immunocompromised hosts with clinically significant (eg, fever, signs of
respiratory compromise) pneumonias. For patients with an endotracheal tube in place,
specific microbial diagnosis may involve early flexible bronchoscopy for bronchoalveolar
lavage with viral, fungal, and bacterial diagnostic studies. Although the protected specimen
brush technique has been utilized in some settings, quantitative bacterial cultures are more
commonly used to differentiate colonization from true lower respiratory tract infection. (See
"Flexible bronchoscopy in adults: Indications and contraindications", section on 'Diagnostic
indications' and "Clinical presentation and diagnostic evaluation of ventilator-associated
pneumonia", section on 'Diagnostic evaluation' and "Community-acquired pneumonia in
children: Clinical features and diagnosis", section on 'Sputum Gram stain and culture'.)
Decisions about appropriate empiric antimicrobial therapy should be made in consultation
with an infectious disease specialist.

   Empiric treatment for pneumonia in immunocompromised hosts requires broad-spectrum
   gram-positive and gram-negative coverage, similar to that required for hospital-acquired
   pneumonia. Immunocompromised patients are also at risk for Pneumocystis jirovecii
   (formerly Pneumocystis carinii). Common respiratory viruses (eg, influenza, RSV, adenovirus,
   severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 [SARS-CoV-2]) may cause serious
   infections in immunocompromised children and may require antiviral treatment if a specific
   etiology is identified. (See 'Confirmed viral etiology' below and "Seasonal influenza in
   children: Management", section on 'Antiviral therapy' and "Respiratory syncytial virus
   infection: Treatment in infants and children", section on 'Immunocompromised patients'.)

PATHOGEN-DIRECTED THERAPY

Once results of microbiologic tests are available, antimicrobial therapy can be directed toward
the responsible pathogen or pathogens.
Confirmed viral etiology — The following viruses should be treated if identified:

●  SARS-CoV-2 – Antiviral therapy is indicated if the child requires supplemental oxygen or
   other respiratory support. (See "COVID-19: Management in children", section on 'Decision
   to start pharmacotherapy'.)

●  Influenza – The diagnosis and treatment of influenza in children are discussed separately.
   (See "Seasonal influenza in children: Management", section on 'Antiviral therapy' and
   "Seasonal influenza in children: Clinical features and diagnosis", section on 'Diagnosis'.)

●  Varicella zoster – Acyclovir is used in the treatment of varicella zoster pneumonia. (See
   "Treatment of varicella (chickenpox) infection".)
In immunocompromised children, antivirals and/or immunotherapy may be used when the
following viruses are identified:

●  Herpes simplex virus – Acyclovir can be used in the treatment of pneumonia due to herpes
   simplex virus (see "Approach to the immunocompromised patient with fever and
   pulmonary infiltrates")

●  Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – Ribavirin therapy with or without nirsevimab (see
   "Respiratory syncytial virus infection: Treatment in infants and children", section on
   'Immunocompromised patients')

●  Parainfluenza – Ribavirin therapy (see "Parainfluenza viruses in children", section on
   'Treatment')

Duration of treatment

●  Parenteral antibiotic duration – There are few data to guide decisions about the duration
   of parenteral therapy for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) [2,60]. It is common to
   switch from parenteral antibiotics to oral therapy once the patient is clinically improving,
   afebrile for 24 to 48 hours, and not vomiting [61].

●  Total antibiotic duration – The total duration of the antibiotic course is determined by the
   severity of the pneumonia, the causative agent, and the immune status of the host.
   There are few randomized controlled trials available to guide decisions about the
   appropriate duration of antimicrobial therapy for radiographically confirmed childhood
   pneumonia that requires hospitalization [2].

   •  Uncomplicated CAP – For children hospitalized with uncomplicated CAP, we generally
      treat with a five- to seven-day course of combined parenteral and oral therapy.
      This is supported by studies demonstrating the effectiveness of shorter courses of
      therapy for uncomplicated pneumonia [62-64]. In a single-center observational study in
      children ≥6 months of age who were hospitalized with uncomplicated CAP, rates of
      treatment failure were similar among those who received antibiotic therapy for 5 to 7
      days and 8 to 14 days (3 versus 6 percent; odds ratio [OR] 0.48, 95% CI 0.18-1.20) [62].

      outpatient visits, readmission, or death within 30 days after completion of antibiotics.

# **No pathogen identified** — If diagnostic studies fail to identify an etiology of the pneumonia and the patient is clinically improving, transition to an oral antibiotic with the same spectrum of activity as the parenteral antibiotic that the patient is receiving.

## ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS

### Duration of treatment

- **Parenteral antibiotic duration** – There are few data to guide decisions about the duration of parenteral therapy for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) [2,60]. It is common to switch from parenteral antibiotics to oral therapy once the patient is clinically improving, afebrile for 24 to 48 hours, and not vomiting [61].

- **Total antibiotic duration** – The total duration of the antibiotic course is determined by the severity of the pneumonia, the causative agent, and the immune status of the host.

There are few randomized controlled trials available to guide decisions about the appropriate duration of antimicrobial therapy for radiographically confirmed childhood pneumonia that requires hospitalization [2].

- **Uncomplicated CAP** – For children hospitalized with uncomplicated CAP, we generally treat with a five- to seven-day course of combined parenteral and oral therapy.

This is supported by studies demonstrating the effectiveness of shorter courses of therapy for uncomplicated pneumonia [62-64]. In a single-center observational study in children ≥6 months of age who were hospitalized with uncomplicated CAP, rates of treatment failure were similar among those who received antibiotic therapy for 5 to 7 days and 8 to 14 days (3 versus 6 percent; odds ratio [OR] 0.48, 95% CI 0.18-1.20) [62]. Treatment failure was defined as a composite of unanticipated emergency department or outpatient visits, readmission, or death within 30 days after completion of antibiotics.

In a subsequent trial, patients with uncomplicated CAP who were randomly assigned to receive 5 days of antibiotics had a similar response to those assigned to receive 10 days of antibiotics [64]. Additionally, fewer patients who received the shorter course of antibiotics had antibiotic resistance genes detected on end-of-treatment throat swabs.

Randomized trials in adult patients with mild to moderate CAP also suggest that outcomes in patients treated for less than seven days are similar to those in patients treated longer. These trials are discussed separately. (See "Treatment of community-acquired pneumonia in adults in the outpatient setting", section on 'Duration of therapy'.)

    course of antibiotic therapy [65]. The duration is determined by the clinical response but
    is usually either a total of three to four weeks or another two weeks after the patient is
    afebrile and has improved clinically. Some infectious disease specialists use an
    erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) value of <20 mm/hour as a laboratory indicator that

Response to therapy — The following clinical parameters should be monitored to assess
response to treatment [1,2]:

●  Temperature

●  Respiratory rate

●  Heart rate

●  Peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2)

●  Work of breathing (eg, retractions, nasal flaring, grunting)

●  Mental status

●  Ability to maintain oral intake and hydration

●  Chest examination (extent of abnormal or absent breath sounds, extent of dullness to
   percussion)
The frequency of monitoring depends upon the severity of illness. In patients who are
receiving oxygen therapy, SpO2 should be evaluated regularly.
The respiratory status of children with uncomplicated CAP who are appropriately treated
should improve within 48 to 72 hours [1]. However, fevers may persist for several days after
initiation of appropriate therapy [52].
Treatment failure — In children with CAP who fail to improve as anticipated, the following
possibilities must be considered [1,2,66,67]:

●  Alternative or coincident diagnoses (eg, foreign body aspiration) (see "Community-acquired
   pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis", section on 'Differential diagnosis')

●  Ineffective antibiotic coverage (lack of coverage for the actual etiology or resistant
   organism)

●  Development of complications (see "Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical
   features and diagnosis", section on 'Complications')

●  Underlying immunodeficiency condition

The history should be reviewed with special attention to the possibility of foreign body
aspiration and geographic or environmental exposures associated with pathogens not
treated by the empiric regimen (    table 9).
A repeat peripheral white blood cell (WBC) count and inflammatory markers should be sent
because they may provide information about disease progression.
Repeat radiographs or additional imaging studies should be obtained to help assess the
degree of parenchymal involvement and evaluate for complications or anatomic
abnormalities [1].
If not already completed, a microbiologic evaluation should be done to help direct antibiotic
therapy. (See "Community-acquired pneumonia in children: Clinical features and diagnosis",
section on 'Microbiologic testing'.)
Invasive procedures may be necessary to obtain lower respiratory tract specimens for culture
and other studies in children in whom an etiologic diagnosis is necessary and has not been
established by other means. These procedures are typically reserved for seriously ill patients
whose condition is worsening despite empiric therapy, individuals with significant
comorbidities (eg, immune compromise), and those with complications [68-71] as follows:

●  Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) – For samples obtained via bronchoscopy,
   quantitative culture techniques are suggested to differentiate true infection from upper
   airway contamination [72-74].

Discharge criteria — Discharge criteria for children who have been admitted to the hospital
with CAP have not been standardized but typically include [1,52]:

●  Vital signs have improved

●  Child is able to maintain adequate fluid and nutrition orally

●  Improvement in respiratory status has improved

●  SpO2 is ≥90 percent in room air

●  Overall clinical status has improved, including level of activity and appetite

●  Afebrile or decreased fever for at least 12 to 24 hours

●  Mental status is stable and at baseline

●  Caregiver is able to administer home antibiotic regimen, and child is able to comply with
   therapy

●  Child can be discharged to a safe and compliant home environment

Outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy (OPAT) is an option for selected patients who
require prolonged parenteral treatment (usually for complicated CAP that for some reason
cannot be treated with an oral antibiotic) and have stabilized clinically [52,81,82]. Eligibility for
OPAT requires a suitable home environment and a pharmacologic agent with a reasonable
dosing schedule [83]. Decisions regarding OPAT should involve the caregivers, an infectious
diseases specialist (or clinician knowledgeable about the use of antimicrobial agents in OPAT),
a hospital pharmacist, and the primary care provider. The services of a visiting nurse may be
required for home visits, education of caregiver(s) and observation of caregiver
administration, and/or obtaining blood samples for therapeutic monitoring.
Follow-up and prognosis

● Follow-up

   •  Primary care follow-up – Children with pneumonia should be seen by their primary care
      provider soon after discharge to ensure that clinical improvement continues and
      antibiotic therapy is being taken as prescribed without ill effects [52]. Decisions regarding

      include the clinical status of the child at the time of discharge.

   •  Resolution of symptoms – Children who are appropriately treated for pneumonia should
      gradually improve with time. Cough may persist for as long as three to four months after
      viral pneumonia. Children who are recovering from typical or atypical bacterial
      pneumonia may continue to cough for several weeks and have moderate dyspnea on

   •  Radiographs – Follow-up radiographs are not necessary in asymptomatic children with
      uncomplicated CAP, including round pneumonia [85]. However, in children with
      complicated pneumonia, particularly those who required invasive interventions, follow-up
      radiographs help to ensure resolution [2]. Follow-up radiographs may also be helpful in
      children with recurrent pneumonia, persistent symptoms, severe atelectasis, or unusually
      located infiltrates [2]. When follow-up radiographs are indicated, they should be obtained
      two to three weeks after hospital discharge.
      Several studies have evaluated the utility of follow-up radiographs in cohorts of children
      with acute radiologically proven CAP [86-91]. Three of the studies included clinical as well
      as radiologic follow-up at three to seven weeks after initial diagnosis [86-89]. In each of
      these studies, follow-up radiographs were normal or improved in asymptomatic children.
      Residual radiographic findings, even when present, did not result in additional therapy.
      Conditions that should be considered if symptoms persist in children with round
      pneumonia include congenital lung sequestration, pulmonary arteriovenous
      malformation, metastatic Wilms tumor, cavitary necrosis, pleural pseudocyst, and
      primary lung carcinoma [85,92-96].

●  Prognosis – Most otherwise healthy children with pneumonia recover without sequelae,
   even if the pneumonia is complicated [52,79,80,97]. In a multicenter cohort study,
   approximately 3 percent of 82,566 children hospitalized with pneumonia were readmitted
   with pneumonia within 30 days of discharge; 8 percent were readmitted for any reason.
   Readmission was more common among children younger than one year of age and
   children with chronic medical conditions [98].
   Although some data suggest that nearly one-half of children who are hospitalized for viral
   pneumonia have symptoms of asthma five years after hospitalization, it is not clear
   whether this is related to unrecognized asthma at the time of presentation with pneumonia
   or a causal relationship between community-acquired viral pneumonia and development of
   asthma [99,100].
   The overall pneumonia mortality rate in resource-abundant countries is <1 per 1000 per
   year [51,101]. Pneumococcal pneumonia case fatality rates (not adjusted for comorbid
   conditions) for children in the United States were estimated to be 4 percent in children
   younger than two years and 2 percent in children 2 to 17 years before the introduction of
   pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) [102].

   The introduction of PCVs has resulted in a dramatic reduction (37 to 80 percent) in invasive
   disease and mortality rates in the countries in which they have been introduced [103].
   However, pneumococcal pneumonia mortality rates have not been specifically examined.
   Data from the United States Pediatric Multicenter Pneumococcal Surveillance Study Group
   demonstrated all-cause pneumococcal mortality rates of 1 percent after the introduction of
   the seven-valent PCV (PCV7; during 2006 to 2009) and 0 percent after the introduction of
   the 13-valent PCV (PCV13; during 2011 to 2014) [104]. In a study from eastern Gambia,
   introduction of a nine-valent PCV was associated with a reduction in all-cause mortality
   from 30.1 to 25.2 per 1000 child-years [105]. (See "Pneumococcal vaccination in children",
   section on 'Efficacy and effectiveness'.)

SOCIETY GUIDELINE LINKS

Links to society and government-sponsored guidelines from selected countries and regions
around the world are provided separately. (See "Society guideline links: Pediatric
pneumonia".)

INFORMATION FOR PATIENTS
UpToDate offers two types of patient education materials, "The Basics" and "Beyond the
Basics." The Basics patient education pieces are written in plain language, at the 5th to 6th
grade reading level, and they answer the four or five key questions a patient might have
about a given condition. These articles are best for patients who want a general overview and
who prefer short, easy-to-read materials. Beyond the Basics patient education pieces are
longer, more sophisticated, and more detailed. These articles are written at the 10th to 12th
grade reading level and are best for patients who want in-depth information and are
comfortable with some medical jargon.
Here are the patient education articles that are relevant to this topic. We encourage you to
print or email these topics to your patients. (You can also locate patient education articles on
a variety of subjects by searching on "patient info" and the keyword[s] of interest.)

Data from the United States Pediatric Multicenter Pneumococcal Surveillance Study Group demonstrated all-cause pneumococcal mortality rates of 1 percent after the introduction of the seven-valent PCV (PCV7; during 2006 to 2009) and 0 percent after the introduction of the 13-valent PCV (PCV13; during 2011 to 2014) [104]. In a study from eastern Gambia, introduction of a nine-valent PCV was associated with a reduction in all-cause mortality from 30.1 to 25.2 per 1000 child-years [105]. (See "Pneumococcal vaccination in children", section on 'Efficacy and effectiveness'.)

●  Pretreatment evaluation – The pretreatment evaluation includes a complete blood count
   (CBC), inflammatory markers, serum electrolytes, chest radiographs, and a microbiologic
   evaluation. (See 'Pretreatment evaluation' above.)

●  Infection control – In addition to standard precautions, transmission-based infection
   control measures vary based on the microbial etiology of CAP. Rapid diagnostic tests may
   help with infection control decisions. (See 'Infection control measures' above.)

●  Supportive care – Supportive care for children hospitalized with pneumonia includes
   provision of antipyresis, analgesia, respiratory support, and fluid management. (See
   'Supportive and adjunctive care' above.)

●  Empiric antimicrobial therapy – Children who are hospitalized with CAP are initially
   treated empirically pending results of microbiologic testing.
   Our suggested approach is as follows (  table 3A-B):

   •  Infants ≥4 weeks to <6 months with nonsevere uncomplicated CAP – For most infants
      ≥4 weeks to <6 months of age who are hospitalized with uncomplicated CAP, we suggest
      treatment with ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (where available) rather than other antibiotics
      (Grade 2C). Infants at this age are not fully immunized and are at risk for penicillin-
      resistant strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae (PRSP) and beta-lactamase-producing
      strains of Haemophilus influenzae, and ceftriaxone and cefotaxime provide excellent
      coverage. The table provides dosing guidance (  table 3B).

   •  Infants and children ≥6 months with nonsevere uncomplicated CAP – Our suggested
      approach for infants and children ≥6 months of age is as follows (See 'Infants and
      children 6 months to <4 years' above and 'Children ≥4 years' above.):
       -  For children with presumed typical bacterial CAP who are fully immunized (  table 5)
          and live in a community with rates of PRSP <25 percent, we suggest ampicillin or
          penicillin G rather than other antibiotics (Grade 2C).
       -  For children who are not fully immunized (  table 5) or live in a community with rates
          of PRSP ≥25 percent, we suggest ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime, where available) rather
          than ampicillin or penicillin G (Grade 2C). (See 'Infants and children 6 months to <4
          years' above and 'Children ≥4 years' above.)
       -  For children <4 years old who have findings consistent with atypical pneumonia (eg,
          myalgias, conjunctivitis, sore throat, rash), we suggest combination therapy with a
          macrolide (eg, azithromycin) plus a beta-lactam (ampicillin, penicillin G, or ceftriaxone)
          (Grade 2C). (See 'Infants and children 6 months to <4 years' above.)

•  Aspiration pneumonia – For children who are hospitalized for aspiration pneumonia, we
   suggest empiric treatment with ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin (Grade 2C). The
   former provides coverage for oral anaerobes as well as the usual bacterial causes of CAP
   (eg, S. pneumoniae, group A Streptococcus [GAS], methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus
   aureus [MSSA], H. influenzae). The latter's coverage is similar except it lacks H. influenzae
   coverage, and its coverage against GAS, S. pneumoniae, and MSSA is not as broad. (See
   'Aspiration pneumonia' above.)

•  Severe and/or complicated pneumonia – Our suggested approach to treating severe or
   complicated pneumonia in children is as follows:
    -  Severe uncomplicated CAP, not critically ill – For children with severe uncomplicated
       CAP (        table 2) who do not require admission to the pediatric intensive care unit
       (PICU), we suggest combination empiric therapy with a third-generation cephalosporin
       (eg, ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) plus a macrolide (eg, azithromycin) (  table 3A-B). (See
       'Severe uncomplicated pneumonia' above.)
    -  Severe CAP, critically ill – For critically ill children requiring PICU care for severe
       pneumonia, we suggest combination therapy with ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime, where
       available) plus vancomycin plus either nafcillin or oxacillin plus azithromycin rather
       than other regimens (Grade 2C). Alternative options for patients with contraindications
       to vancomycin or beta-lactams are provided above. (See 'Severe uncomplicated
       pneumonia' above.)
    -  Parapneumonic effusion/empyema or necrotizing pneumonia – For patients with
       parapneumonic effusion/empyema or necrotizing pneumonia, we suggest combination
       therapy with ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime, where available) plus either clindamycin or
       vancomycin rather than other regimens (Grade 2C). (See 'Complicated pneumonia'
       above.)

Alternative options for patients with contraindications to vancomycin or beta-lactams are provided above. (See 'Severe uncomplicated pneumonia' above.)

      -  Lung abscess – For patients with lung abscess, we suggest either monotherapy with
         ampicillin-sulbactam or combination therapy with ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime, where
         available) plus clindamycin (vancomycin is an alternative if the prevalence of
         clindamycin resistance in the community is ≥15 percent) rather than other regimens
         (Grade 2C). (See 'Complicated pneumonia' above.)

   •  Hospital-acquired pneumonia – For patients with hospital-acquired pneumonia, we
      suggest empiric treatment with piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, or cefepime (Grade
      2C). For children in whom methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) is suspected, we suggest
      the addition of vancomycin or linezolid to the regimen (Grade 2C). (See 'Hospital-acquired
      pneumonia' above.)

   •  Immunocompromised host – Immunocompromised children who are hospitalized with
      pneumonia require broad-spectrum empiric coverage. Consultation with an infectious
      disease specialist is advised. (See 'Immunocompromised host' above.)

●  Pathogen-directed therapy – If microbiologic testing identifies a specific pathogen,
   antibiotic therapy is directed toward the specific pathogen. (See 'Pathogen-directed therapy'
   above.)

●  Duration of treatment – Parenteral therapy is typically transitioned to oral therapy when
   the patient has been afebrile for 24 to 48 hours and can tolerate oral intake. The total
   duration of antibiotic therapy is usually five to seven days for uncomplicated CAP. Up to four
   weeks of antimicrobial therapy may be necessary for complicated CAP. (See 'Duration of
   treatment' above.)

●  Treatment failure – The respiratory status of children receiving appropriate antimicrobial
   therapy for CAP should improve within 48 to 72 hours. Children who fail to improve as
   anticipated may not be receiving adequate antibiotic therapy, may have developed
   complications, or may have an alternative or coincident diagnosis. (See 'Treatment failure'
   above.)

●  Follow-up and prognosis – Children recovering from CAP may continue to cough for
   several weeks to four months, depending upon the etiology. Those recovering from typical
   or atypical bacterial pneumonia may also have moderate dyspnea on exertion for two to
   three months. After this recovery period, most otherwise healthy children do not have any
   long-term sequelae. (See 'Follow-up and prognosis' above.)
   Follow-up radiographs are not necessary in asymptomatic children with uncomplicated CAP,
   including round pneumonia. However, in children with complicated pneumonia, especially
   those who required intervention, follow-up radiographs help to ensure resolution. (See
   'Follow-up and prognosis' above.)

community. Additional considerations in the decision to choose vancomycin include the prevalence of
MRSA in the community, the severity of illness, and the turn-around time for susceptibilities.
Δ If tolerated, oral therapy is recommended.
◊ Nafcillin is added if S. aureus is likely because MSSA is more rapidly killed by nafcillin than by
vancomycin.
§ Ampicillin-sulbactam alone may be effective if lung abscess is thought to be secondary to aspiration.

Consultation with a specialist in pediatric infectious diseases is suggested for children with severe
hypersensitivity to beta-lactam antibiotics (eg, penicillins and cephalosporins) and for
immunocompromised children. The recommended doses are for children with normal kidney function.

IV: intravenous; MRSA: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
* Class Ia antiarrhythmic drugs include quinidine, ajmaline, disopyramide, and procainamide.
¶ Alternative dosing is suggested for clinicians/institutions who follow AUC-guided therapeutic
monitoring for vancomycin for serious MRSA infections as suggested by consensus guidelines [4] ; this
strategy requires input from a clinical pharmacist, who will provide recommendations for initial dosing.
Refer to UpToDate content on invasive staphylococcal infections in children for details of trough-
guided and AUC-guided vancomycin dosing.

items.md: <sup>Δ</sup> Children at high risk for invasive Hib disease include chemotherapy recipients and those living with anatomic or functional asplenia (including sickle cell disease), HIV infection, immunoglobulin deficiency, or early component complement deficiency. Please refer to the UpToDate topic on prevention of *H. influenzae* infection for a discussion of full Hib immunization in children at high risk for invasive Hib disease.
items.value: <sup>Δ</sup> Children at high risk for invasive Hib disease include chemotherapy recipients and those living with anatomic or functional asplenia (including sickle cell disease), HIV infection, immunoglobulin deficiency, or early component complement deficiency. Please refer to the UpToDate topic on prevention of *H. influenzae* infection for a discussion of full Hib immunization in children at high risk for invasive Hib disease.

items.md: <sup>◇</sup> Children at high risk for invasive *S. pneumoniae* disease include those with chronic heart disease (particularly cyanotic congenital heart disease and cardiac failure); chronic lung disease (including asthma if treated with high-dose oral corticosteroid therapy); diabetes mellitus; cerebrospinal fluid leak; cochlear implant; sickle cell disease and other hemoglobinopathies; anatomic or functional asplenia; HIV infection; chronic kidney failure; nephrotic syndrome; diseases associated with treatment with immunosuppressive drugs or radiation therapy, including malignant neoplasms, leukemias, lymphomas, and Hodgkin disease; solid organ transplantation; or congenital immunodeficiency. Please refer to the UpToDate topics on PCVs and pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccines for a discussion of full *S. pneumoniae* immunization in children at high risk for invasive *S. pneumoniae* disease.
